channel.title: Nonclusive by Design, writing
channel.description: Nonclusive by Design newsletter editions and essays on accessibility, usability and Universal Design.

item.title: When the Accessible Route Is the Main Route
item.description: I was recently in Denmark to be inaugurated as a Bevica Guest Professor in Universal Design at the Kolding School of Design. I went there together with my family, and we also had a full day at LEGO House in Billund.

item.title: What If We Leave the Circle Open?
item.description: Summer to me means spending time outdoors. Having a break now and then. Dwelling. But where? Some furniture is like open arms, waiting for you. Some is closed, leaving no openings.

item.title: Design Can Protect and Support Dignity, But Not Create It
item.description: Every person has inherent worth and dignity simply by being born. It exists whether or not design acknowledges it. But every design decision can either recognise and support that existing dignity, or undermine and violate it.

item.title: The Lazarus Door – What Inclusion Actually Is
item.description: I recently saw Wake Up Dead Man – A Knives Out Mystery. It was a good film, and one thing in particular stayed with me: the Lazarus door to the Wicks' mausoleum. It took me until the day after to figure out why I couldn't let go of that do…

item.title: Spring Challenge – Can You Photograph Belonging?
item.description: It is springtime in Sweden, and we are starting to spend more time outside. I have a challenge for you. The next time you go for a walk, look at the spaces around you, and try to photograph belonging. And if you travel, you naturally pay m…

item.title: Benchmarking Universal Design – Are We Looking in the Right Place?
item.description: Have you ever found yourself in a situation where you started to discuss how to evaluate Universal Design and ended up discussing ramps and other accessibility features? I have. Many times.

item.title: On Being Disablised – What 57 000 Media Articles Say About Society
item.description: I made this photo collage to capture a feeling: the experience of being "disablised."

item.title: What If Universal Design Were Always Nonclusive?
item.description: Every few years, I return to a chapter I first read as a fresh PhD student in 2006. Edward Steinfeld and Beth Tauke's "Universal Designing"[2] was part of a remarkable period for the field. When someone asks me about a key era in Universal…

item.title: Vibrating Inequality – Testimonial from an iPhone
item.description: Hello there 👋 Disability studies has long argued for centring lived experience. But it can be hard to fully convey what it feels like to move through a city in a wheelchair. This newsletter describes an experiment in making the invisible v…

item.title: What "Not Yet" Denies, "Already" Can Change
item.description: In newsletter #8, I wrote about a situation on board a train, where I was placed in a separate space that felt like a luggage compartment (Figure 1). It became my most shared post so far, and something clearly resonated.

item.title: One Word for Universal Design: "Togetherness"
item.description: This is this year’s final edition, written as we head into a season that reminds us of the value of togetherness.

item.title: Say "I Already Belong" And The Conditional Access Paradigm Crumbles
item.description: Lately, I’ve been trying to work through the consequences of the statement “I already belong”.

item.title: Why Getting from A to B Isn't Enough – Understanding Accessibility, Usability, and Universal Design
item.description: Universal Design goes beyond accessibility. This story shows how design choices shape dignity and diversity, and how getting from point A to B isn't enough.

item.title: How Categorisation Shapes (and Limits) Universal Design
item.description: Why do we have different signs for "disabled toilet" and "toilet"? Why not just "Large" and "Small" toilets? This suggestion has been around since the 1970s, but still awaits its breakthrough.

item.title: Why Do We Grab Our Cameras When Something Feels Wrong – Or Right?
item.description: My work often starts with a photo.

item.title: Who Are All These "Others" In Policy Texts?
item.description: Have you noticed how often the word "others" appears in policy texts? My previous articles dealt with "us and them" divisions in signs and the built environment.

item.title: Who Carries the Burden When Design Fails?
item.description: Using a red carpet on an inaccessible staircase effectively places a person using a wheelchair, like me, as “abnormal”. The red carpet on this hotel's stairs clearly wasn't rolled out for me (Picture 1).

item.title: Three Strategies Designers Use To Acknowledge Diversity
item.description: I love toilet signs. They say a lot about our society and how people think.

item.title: Why "Nonclusion"?
item.description: I got a question in a comment that inspired this post: Why did you choose the term “nonclusion”? Good question!

item.title: Design beyond "us" and "them"
item.description: Design is powerful. It shapes how we move, connect, and participate. Too often, it silently follows norms that exclude, creating experiences of "us" and "them".

item.title: Peekaboo! The Joke That Showed How Exclusion Makes Everyone Poorer – Including the Included
item.description: The moment I stepped onto the stage to begin my presentation on Universal Design, I stared at a huge monster of a fixed speaker podium that stood between me and the audience.

item.title: One Goal, Three Names: Why I Don’t Separate Universal, Inclusive, or Design for All
item.description: I enjoy a good conceptual discussion just as much as anyone else, but not when it comes to the three siblings: “Universal Design”, “Inclusive Design” and “Design for all”.

item.description: Design can be brutal in how it affects people.

item.title: A View into a Different World, where Accessibility is the Norm
item.description: Imagine a place where human diversity is expected and accessibility is the norm. There are such pockets of society, but they are few and far between. Hotel Ilunion Malaga is one of them.

item.title: Universal Design—A Shift in Culture? (Keynote Lecture)
item.description: Does Universal Design demand a cultural transformation to succeed? My short answer would be “Yes!”.
